title: "E.1.7 Authorship of Natural Evil"

Natural evil is the suffering built into the world's workings rather than chosen by any creature: predation, parasitism, disease, congenital disorder, the long catalogue of animal pain that ran for hundreds of millions of years before any moral agent was on the scene. It is the residue the free-will defense never reaches (no free creaturely choice stands between God and it) and the residue the Fall cannot reach either, since the suffering predates any embodied will that could have fallen (see *The Fall*, and *The Soul-Making Theodicy* on the pre-human front). Stripped of both buffers, natural evil is the cleanest case of the question the excursus presses on every theodicy: if the suffering was built into the design, who authored it? This entry runs that question to its end, the design-authorship line, for the evil that has no candidate author but the design.

*The three layers of design.* The theist who concedes that natural suffering is built in, not chosen, still hopes to keep it from being God's intended feature. Three layers must each be cleared, and each is authored. The first is the *capacity* to suffer: a nervous system that registers damage as agony rather than as neutral signal. That capacity was designed: a creature could have been built to track injury as information without the felt torment. The second is the *inescapability* of that suffering for the creature that has it: the animal cannot opt out of its nociception, cannot revise its own design. Grant both, and the defender's last move is that the suffering is inescapable *as such*, fixed by the nature of embodied life. But inescapability-for-the-creature is not inescapability-for-the-designer: what the animal cannot revise, the designer chose not to revise. The third layer is therefore *design-level gratuity*: a suffering escapable at the level of design but made inescapable for the creature is not a constraint the designer suffered but a feature the designer selected. Each layer the defender concedes pushes the authorship up one level, and the top level is the design itself.

*The appeal to law, and the fork it opens.* The standing reply is that the layers are not chosen but fixed: a law-governed world of the kind embodied life requires simply comes with damage, predation, and pain, and God could no more omit them than draw a round square. Ask where the necessity of these laws resides, and the reply forks. If God could have set different laws, then the law-package that makes suffering necessary was itself among his options, and choosing it is choosing the suffering it entails: the necessity is real, but it is the designer's own stipulation, authored one level up. If God could not, because the laws are a material he did not make and cannot alter, then he is a craftsman ordering a recalcitrant given, a demiurge, not the omnipotent creator *ex nihilo* the theodicy needs — the necessity is real, but the price is the very omnipotence the defense was built to protect. There is a third reading, and it is the one classical theism actually holds: the laws could not be otherwise because they flow necessarily from God's own nature — binding on him, and in that sense unchosen, yet not imposed on him from outside. This is the strongest form of the reply, and it does not break the dilemma but deepens it. If the laws, and the suffering they entail, follow necessarily from what God *is*, then that suffering is entailed by God's very nature — not selected by his will, but authored beneath the level of will, in the divine essence itself; the believer who adopts this position does not move the suffering away from God but roots it in him. So the fork closes from every side: laws God chose author the suffering by choice, laws flowing from God's nature author it by nature, and only laws external to God break the authorship — at the price of the omnipotence the whole defense rests on.

*The biological exhibit.* The claim that consumptive, predatory suffering is a necessity of *any* living world is empirically false on the tradition's own creation. Autotrophs (the photosynthetic and chemosynthetic organisms at the base of every food web) sustain themselves without consuming other life at all; an entire living order runs on non-consumptive metabolism. A biosphere need not be predatory to exist: predation is a contingent feature of *this* design, not a thermodynamic requirement of life as such. The exhibit does not need the maximal claim that life could be made wholly undamageable; it needs only the modest, demonstrated one — that the consumptive arms race of tooth and claw is one option among others a designer had, which redirects every appeal to its necessity back into the change-the-laws fork above. The exhibit answers the *nomological* necessity claim — that a living world must run on consumption. A different necessity is sometimes pressed in its place: Swinburne's argument that natural evil is required for *knowledge*, since significant free agency needs agents who can learn from regular natural processes how their actions bring benefit and harm, and that knowledge has to be bought with real instances of natural suffering (Swinburne 1998). Grant the connection in full; it does not break the fork but chooses a horn within it. A world in which significant agency *requires* built-in suffering as its price is itself one design among the options the autotrophic base shows a creator was not forced into — so selecting the suffering-priced world for the agency it buys is choosing the suffering for the work it does, which is precisely the horn on which suffering that does justifying work is a chosen feature of the design, authored by the designer who valued what it purchases.

*The anti-coercion exhibit.* The same test applies to a narrower and more exacting case: the vulnerability of an embodied reproductive system to insemination the bearer does not consent to. If a body capable of sexual reproduction is thereby, of necessity, a body with no way to block that specific harm, the vulnerability is a cost of reproduction as such, not a further design choice layered on top of it. The claim is false on the same evidentiary ground the autotrophic case uses: contingent, currently existing lineages carry real defenses against exactly this harm, defenses too heterogeneous in mechanism and too uneven in distribution to be a side effect of anything reproduction as such requires. Waterfowl vaginal tracts have coevolved corkscrewing, dead-end pouches running counter to the male's coiled phallus — structures that impede full penetration precisely in forced matings, and whose complexity tracks, across species, the rate at which females are subject to forced extra-pair copulation (Brennan and Prum 2015). Across primates and beyond, behavioral and physiological counter-strategies to sexual coercion — mate-guarding evasion, coalition formation, cryptic control of paternity — recur wherever the selective pressure that would favor them is present (Smit 2025). None of this is one mechanism generalized; it is convergent pressure answered independently, again and again, wherever a lineage's circumstances favored it — and sometimes answered the other way: the copulatory tie of canids locks the pair together for the male's benefit, not the female's (Dewsbury 1972), confirming that the direction an arms race like this runs is itself a further design fact, not a forced outcome of embodiment. The choice tracks no principle a defender could retreat to. Orangutans — great apes, among humanity's nearest surviving relatives — face frequent forced copulation from unflanged males; females deploy behavioral counter-tactics (seeking proximity to protective dominant males) but no anatomical mechanism comparable to the duck's vaginal counter-morphology is documented in the lineage (Knott 2009). Phylogenetic closeness to humans, then, predicts nothing about whether the physiological layer of the defense is present. It is fixed lineage by lineage, which is what a design-level choice looks like and not what a nomological necessity does. Applied to the three layers above: the capacity to be violated by forced insemination with no bodily recourse at all is not the only option a designer had; the option was demonstrably available, since it is instantiated right now in cousin lineages; and withholding it from the one lineage capable of reflecting on the fact is a design-level choice like any other — gratuitous unless it does the same justifying work the knowledge-buying reply claimed for suffering in general, which is the horn the fork above has already closed.

*Why the line bites here and not elsewhere.* Against *moral* evil the theist has a real buffer: the free-will defense interposes a created will between God and the harm, so that the suffering traces to the creature's choice rather than to the design (the book contests that defense on other grounds, but the buffer at least exists). Natural evil has no such buffer. There is no free creature whose choice produced the earthquake or the parasite; there is no fallen will upstream of the Cambrian; there is no developing subject being formed by suffering that ran before subjects existed. Every device the other theodicies use to relocate authorship away from the design is unavailable, because the only candidate author left in the frame *is* the design. One move tries to restore the missing buffer: the Augustinian free-will theodicy Plantinga revives in *God, Freedom, and Evil* (Plantinga 1974a), on which natural evil traces to the free choices of nonhuman creatures — fallen angels whose rebellion predates and corrupts the natural order, supplying exactly the will upstream of the Cambrian that the design-authorship line says is absent. Grant it its best case. It still does not relocate the authorship; it moves it up one agent and returns it unchanged. A created will, angelic or otherwise, acts in Time, occupies Space, and persists as a bearer — it stands inside the design, not behind it, and an agent inside the design can no more author the capacity to suffer, the inescapability of that capacity, or the law-package that fixes both than a creature can write its own nociception into being. What a fallen will could do is actualize cruelties the design already made available; what it could not do is author the design that made them available. So the move faces the same fork as the appeal to law: either the angelic will works with a nature God set, and the three layers are authored exactly as before, or it works with a nature God did not set, which is the demiurge horn again, omnipotence traded away. The interposed will postpones the question by one agent; it does not answer it. So the gratuity-or-authorship dilemma stated for theodicy generally (see *The Soul-Making Theodicy*) does not merely apply to natural evil — it has nowhere else to land: either the built-in suffering does no justifying work, in which case it is gratuitous, or it does, in which case it is a chosen feature of the design and authored by the designer.

*What this leaves the defender.* The honest fallback is to drop the necessity claim and own the design — to grant that the suffering is built in and intended, and to carry the burden of squaring an intended, creature-borne agony with the goodness the tradition ascribes to its author. That is the evidential problem of evil returned in its sharpest form, no longer softened by free will, by a fall, or by law. The skeptical-theist retreat to reasons past our grasp is closed upstream once the good has been named: a defense may not appeal to a good it also declares beyond assessment. What remains, as with the soul-making theodicy, is suffering the design permits but cannot disown — except that here, with every buffer removed, it traces back to the designer.

*What is challenged.* Natural evil raises an especially difficult authorship question for creator theism: a theology must explain the capacity for suffering, the relevant laws, and their distribution without simply relocating responsibility. The design-authorship argument is strongest where a tradition attributes exhaustive creative control; it weakens where the theology revises omnipotence, adopts independent constraints, or disputes the proposed alternatives. The chapter argues that standard free-will and fall accounts do not by themselves settle the problem, rather than proving that every possible theodicy assigns direct intending will to God.
